name: Basics
description: A guided AI workflow: brainstorm → plan → build → verify → ship. Plus the full git workflow, repo setup helpers, and documentation actions.

actions.label: Brainstorm
actions.description: Refine the idea before any code.
actions.template: Help me brainstorm this. Ask me what I'm trying to build, surface my assumptions, and suggest two or three approaches with their tradeoffs. Don't write any code yet — we're refining the design first.

actions.label: Write plan
actions.description: Turn the design into a step-by-step implementation plan.
actions.template: We have a design. Write a step-by-step implementation plan to docs/plan.md that an engineer without project context could follow — exact file paths, complete code snippets, verification steps. Don't write the implementation yet.

actions.label: Build (TDD)
actions.description: Implement the next task with test-driven development.
actions.template: Implement the next task from the plan using test-driven development: write the failing test first, run it to confirm it fails, then write the minimum code to make it pass. Commit at each step.

actions.label: Debug
actions.template: Something is broken. Investigate systematically: reproduce the issue first, then form a hypothesis, then test it. Don't guess at fixes without evidence — find the root cause before changing anything.

actions.label: Verify
actions.description: Run all the project's checks and fix failures.
actions.template: Verify this work is actually complete. Run the project's checks (lint, typecheck, tests — whatever the README or CLAUDE.md mentions). Fix every failure. Don't claim done until everything passes.

actions.label: Self-review
actions.description: Read your own changes carefully before asking anyone else to.
actions.template: Self-review the changes on this branch. Read every modified file, compare against the plan, and list anything missing, redundant, or sub-par with file:line references. Then fix it.

actions.label: Triage PR comments
actions.description: Read PR review comments and propose what to do about each, written to .broomy/output/feedback.md.
actions.template:
Read the review comments on the open PR for this branch and propose a plan for each one. Don't implement anything yet — this is the triage step.

1. Run `gh pr view --json number,url,reviews,comments` to get the PR. Run `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/pulls/<PR_NUMBER>/comments` to fetch inline (line-level) review comments.
2. For each comment (both general review comments and inline file/line comments), capture: the commenter, the file path and line range (if any), the comment body, and what the commenter is asking for or pointing out.
3. For each one, propose a response with technical rigor — do NOT blindly agree:
   - **Agree and implement**: include a brief sketch of what you'd change
   - **Disagree because …**: explain why, citing code or constraints
   - **Need clarification**: name the specific question
   - **Already addressed in <commit-sha or file:line>**: link to where
4. Write the result to `.broomy/output/feedback.md` as a markdown document. Group comments by file. For each comment, include: who said what (with quote), your proposed response, and an action line at the bottom.
5. Do NOT change any code in this step. The user reviews `.broomy/output/feedback.md` first; the 'Address feedback' action implements afterwards.

actions.label: Address feedback
actions.description: Implement the triage plan written by 'Triage PR comments'.
actions.template:
Read `.broomy/output/feedback.md` — it contains the triaged plan for each PR comment. Implement the items marked 'Agree and implement', skip those marked 'Disagree' or 'Already addressed', and for 'Need clarification' items ask the user before doing anything.

For each comment you act on, decide with technical rigor whether the proposed change is correct — don't just blindly implement what the triage doc says if you spot a problem. Reply to comments you disagree with using `gh api` POST to the review-comment reply endpoint, explaining why. When you push the fixes, the original commenters get notified.

actions.label: Commit
actions.description: Commit current changes with an AI-written message.
actions.template: Look at the current git diff and make a commit. Stage all relevant files, write a clear commit message that describes what changed and why, and commit. Do not commit any files that contain secrets or credentials.

actions.label: Resolve conflicts
actions.description: Resolve merge conflicts cleanly, integrating both sides where appropriate.
actions.template:
Resolve merge conflicts from merging {main} into the current branch.

1. Run `git status` to see conflicted files
2. For each conflict, examine the markers and run `git log --oneline HEAD...MERGE_HEAD -- <file>` to understand both sides
3. If any conflict is ambiguous, ask the user before guessing
4. Edit files to produce correct merged results — integrate both changes where appropriate
5. Run the project's lint/typecheck/test commands to verify everything passes
6. Stage resolved files and commit with `git commit --no-edit`

Never silently discard changes from either side.

actions.label: Sync changes
actions.description: Pull the latest from main, resolve conflicts, validate, and push.
actions.template:
Sync this branch with {main}. Follow these steps in order:

## Step 1: Commit uncommitted work

Run `git status`. If there are staged or unstaged changes (including untracked files that look like project code), stage and commit them with a clear commit message. Do not commit files that contain secrets or credentials. If the working tree is already clean, skip this step.

## Step 2: Pull latest from {main}

Run `git fetch origin {main}` to get the latest state of {main}.

If {main} is already up to date with this branch (i.e. no new commits on origin/{main} since the last merge or branch point), tell the user the branch is already up to date and stop here.

Otherwise, continue.

## Step 3: Understand what changed on {main}

Find the merge base: `git merge-base HEAD origin/{main}`

List PRs merged into {main} since the merge base:
```
gh pr list --state merged --base {main} --search "merged:>$(git log -1 --format=%ci <merge-base>)" --limit 20 --json number,title,author,mergedAt,body
```

Summarize the merged PRs for context (title, author, and a one-line summary of what each changed). This helps understand the intent behind changes that might conflict.

## Step 4: Merge {main} into this branch

Run `git merge origin/{main}`.

If the merge completes cleanly with no conflicts, skip to Step 6.

## Step 5: Resolve conflicts

If there are merge conflicts:

1. Run `git status` to list all conflicted files.
2. For each conflicted file, examine the conflict markers and understand both sides:
   - Run `git log --oneline HEAD...MERGE_HEAD -- <file>` to see the commit history for both sides
   - Use the PR context from Step 3 to understand the *intent* behind the incoming changes
3. Categorize each conflict:
   - **Obvious**: Mechanical conflicts (e.g. both sides added imports, adjacent line changes) — resolve these automatically
   - **Non-obvious**: Semantic conflicts where the correct resolution depends on product intent, or where both sides made deliberate but incompatible changes — ASK THE USER how to resolve these before proceeding
4. Also check for **semantic conflicts** that git won't flag: places where the merge is syntactically clean but the combined code is logically incorrect. For example:
   - A function signature changed on {main} but this branch calls it with the old signature
   - A variable/type was renamed on {main} but this branch references the old name
   - A feature was removed on {main} but this branch extends it
   - Configuration or API changes on {main} that affect code on this branch
   Run `git diff origin/{main}...HEAD` and cross-reference with `git diff $(git merge-base HEAD origin/{main})...origin/{main}` to find these.
5. Fix all conflicts and semantic issues. Stage the resolved files.

## Step 6: Validate

Run the project's validation checks (lint, typecheck, tests). Fix any failures — all checks must pass with zero errors. If you fix anything, amend the merge commit or create a follow-up commit.

## Step 7: Complete the merge

If there were conflicts, complete the merge: `git commit --no-edit`

Then push the branch to its remote tracking branch. If there is no remote tracking branch yet, run `git push -u origin HEAD`.

Summarize what was merged and any conflicts that were resolved.

actions.label: Push branch
actions.description: Push this branch to the remote, fixing any pre-push hook failures.
actions.template: Push this branch to the remote (`git push -u origin HEAD` if there is no tracking branch yet). If the push is rejected by a pre-push hook (lint, type-check, tests, formatter, etc.), read the error output, fix the underlying problem, commit the fix, and push again. Repeat until the push succeeds. Never bypass hooks with --no-verify.

actions.label: Create PR
actions.description: Prepare the branch, open a PR, and watch CI until it's green.
actions.template:
Create a pull request for the current branch against {main}.

## Step 1: Prepare the branch

1. Stage and commit any uncommitted changes. Write a clear commit message describing what changed. Do not commit files that contain secrets or credentials.
2. Pull the latest from {main} and merge it into the current branch: `git fetch origin {main} && git merge origin/{main}`. If there are merge conflicts, resolve them.
3. Run the project's validation checks (lint, typecheck, tests). Fix any failures — all checks must pass with zero errors.
4. Push the branch to its remote tracking branch. If there is no remote tracking branch yet, run `git push -u origin HEAD`.

## Step 2: Create the PR

1. Run `git diff origin/{main}...HEAD` and `git log origin/{main}..HEAD --oneline` to understand the changes
2. Check for a PR template in `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` or similar locations
3. If a template exists, follow it. Otherwise write: Background and Motivation, Design Decisions, Proposed Changes (grouped by pattern, not just file lists), and Testing
4. If this session is linked to an issue, the issue number is: {issueNumber}. If an issue number is present, the FIRST line of the PR body MUST be `Fixes #{issueNumber}` followed by a blank line before the rest of the body
5. Derive a clear title under 70 characters. Check `gh pr list --state merged --limit 5` for style conventions
6. Create the PR with `gh pr create --title "<title>" --body "<body>"`

## Step 3: Wait for CI and fix failures

1. Wait for all CI checks to complete on the PR. Poll with `gh pr checks <number> --watch` or periodically check with `gh pr checks <number>`.
2. If all checks pass, you're done.
3. If any checks fail:
   a. Inspect the failed check logs: `gh run view <run-id> --log-failed`
   b. Diagnose and fix the failures in the code.
   c. Commit the fixes with a clear message describing what was fixed.
   d. Push the fixes to the branch.
   e. Go back to step 1 and wait for CI to run again on the new push.
4. Repeat until all checks pass or you've made 3 fix attempts. If checks still fail after 3 attempts, summarize the remaining failures for the user.

actions.label: Review
actions.description: Code review the current branch and write the result to .broomy/output/review.md.
actions.template:
Review the changes on the current branch against {main}.

1. Run `git fetch origin {main}` to ensure the base branch ref is up to date
2. Run `git diff origin/{main}...HEAD` to see all changes
3. Run `git log origin/{main}..HEAD --oneline` for commit history
4. Run `gh pr view --json number,body` to get the PR number and description.
5. Use the PR number from step 4 to fetch review comments: `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/pulls/<PR_NUMBER>/comments`. Also get your username with `gh api user --jq .login`. If you find previous review comments by you, focus your review on what has changed since your last review (i.e. your most recent review, not anyone else's) and whether your suggested changes were addressed. Pay particular attention to whether comments and requested changes by you (the current user) have been addressed — these are the highest priority.
6. Review the code for: correctness, potential bugs, security issues, performance concerns, and code quality.

IMPORTANT: Every time you reference code in your review, you MUST include a markdown link using the repo-relative file path. Format: `[src/file.tsx:12-45](src/file.tsx#L12-L45)` for a range, or `[src/file.tsx:12](src/file.tsx#L12)` for a single line. Never use GitHub URLs — the UI renders these as clickable links that open an internal diff viewer.

7. Write your review to `.broomy/output/review.md` as a markdown document with these sections:
   - **Change Summary**: Group all changes into logical groups of related changes. For each group, write a short summary of what those changes accomplish and include links to every code change that belongs to that group.
   - **Issues Found**
   - **Suggestions**
   - **Overall Assessment**
   - **Changes Since Your Last Review** (only if you have previously reviewed this PR)

actions.label: Plan issue
actions.description: Read the linked GitHub issue, clarify, then write a plan to .broomy/output/plan.md.
actions.template: Read the issue using `gh issue view {issueNumber}`. Before doing anything, ask me any questions about the issue to clarify requirements and resolve ambiguities. Then write a plan to `.broomy/output/plan.md`.

actions.label: Screenshot walkthrough
actions.description: Build a screenshot-driven walkthrough of what's been created on this branch.
actions.template:
Create a screenshot-based walkthrough that demonstrates what has been built on this branch.

1. Identify the key UI states or completed features that show what the work accomplishes. Look at the changes on this branch (`git diff origin/{main}...HEAD`) to decide what to show.
2. For each, capture a screenshot and write a short caption explaining what the user should notice.
3. Assemble the result as a markdown document at `.broomy/output/walkthrough.md`. Embed screenshot images stored alongside in `.broomy/output/walkthrough/` (e.g. `walkthrough/01-initial.png`).
4. If you don't have a screenshot tool available in this environment, tell me what would be needed (e.g. Playwright, a running dev server) and stop — don't fake the screenshots.

actions.label: Document progress
actions.description: Summarise progress made since the last progress document.
actions.template:
Create or update a progress document at `.broomy/output/progress.md`.

1. Check whether `.broomy/output/progress.md` already exists. If it does, read it to find the date and contents of the most recent entry — that's your previous checkpoint.
2. Summarise what has been accomplished since that checkpoint: new commits (`git log` since the checkpoint date), features added, bugs fixed, decisions made, blockers cleared, anything still open. Be specific and reference files/PRs/issues where relevant.
3. Write the new entry as a dated section (e.g. `## 2026-05-21`) at the TOP of `.broomy/output/progress.md`, keeping all older entries intact below.
4. If the file does not exist yet, create it with a single dated section summarising all the work on this branch so far.
